title: Two Sum
statement: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers that add up to target. Each input has exactly one solution.
hints: A brute-force double loop works but is O(n^2) - can you do better?
As you scan, what would you need to remember to check each number instantly?
Store each value's index in a hash map; for x, look up (target - x).
approach: One pass: for each x, check if complement exists in the map; else store x. Guaranteed one solution.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
statement: Given prices where prices[i] is the day-i price, pick one day to buy and a later day to sell for maximum profit. Return 0 if no profit possible.
hints: Track the lowest price seen so far as you go.
At each day, the best profit ending today = price - min_price_so_far.
Keep a running maximum of that value.
approach: Single left-to-right scan maintaining min_price and max_profit.

title: Maximum Subarray
statement: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return that sum.
hints: Decide at each element: extend the previous subarray or start fresh here.
Keep two numbers: best sum ending at i, and best sum seen anywhere.
This is Kadane's algorithm.
approach: Kadane's algorithm: iterate once, maintaining cur = max(x, cur + x) — the best subarray ending here — and best = max(best, cur) over all positions. Runs in O(n) time, O(1) space.
pitfalls: Resetting cur to 0 breaks all-negative arrays

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement: Given nums, return an array where answer[i] is the product of all elements except nums[i]. No division; O(n) time.
hints: The answer for i = (product of left part) x (product of right part).
Compute left products in a forward pass into the output array.
Then sweep backward multiplying in the right products - O(1) extra space.
approach: Two passes: prefix products into output, then suffix product accumulated backward.
complexity: Time O(n), Space O(1) excluding output
pitfalls: Extra arrays when O(1) space is required

title: 3Sum
statement: Given an integer array nums, return all unique triplets [a, b, c] such that a + b + c = 0. The solution set must not contain duplicate triplets, and triplets may be returned in any order. Aim for better than the naive O(n^3) enumeration.
hints: Sorting first makes duplicates manageable - why?
Fix one element, then use two pointers on the rest like Two Sum II.
Skip equal neighbors after sorting to avoid duplicate triplets.
approach: Sort; for each i, two-pointer scan of (i+1..end); skip duplicates at all three positions.
complexity: Time O(n^2), Space O(1) excluding output

title: Container With Most Water
statement: Given heights, find two lines forming the container holding the most water.
hints: Start with the widest container (both ends) and narrow it.
Which pointer should move - and why is it safe to move it?
Move the shorter side: it can never form a better pair at this width.
approach: Two pointers inward; area = min(h[l],h[r]) * (r-l); move the smaller height.
pitfalls: Moving the taller pointer (loses the proof)

title: Trapping Rain Water
statement: Given an elevation map, compute how much water it traps after raining.
hints: Water at i = min(tallest left, tallest right) - height[i].
Precompute left-max and right-max arrays for an O(n) space solution.
Two pointers can do it in O(1) space: always advance the lower side.
approach: Two pointers with left_max/right_max; add water on the lower side each step.

title: Find the Duplicate Number
statement: Array of n+1 integers in [1, n] with one duplicate. Find it without modifying the array, O(1) space.
hints: Treat values as next-pointers: index i -> nums[i] forms a linked list with a cycle.
The duplicate is the cycle entrance (two numbers point to it).
Apply Floyd's tortoise and hare, then find the entrance.
approach: Phase 1: find meeting point. Phase 2: one pointer to start, move both - they meet at the duplicate.
pitfalls: Binary-search-on-count is O(n log n) - acceptable but not the intended trick

title: First Missing Positive
statement: Find the smallest missing positive integer in an unsorted array. O(n) time, O(1) space.
hints: The answer is in [1, n+1] - so ignore everything else.
Place each x in [1,n] at index x-1 by swapping (cyclic sort).
Then the first index i with nums[i] != i+1 gives the answer.
approach: Cyclic placement pass, then a linear scan for the first misplaced value.
pitfalls: Infinite swap loops (skip when already correct)

title: Merge Intervals
statement: Given an array of intervals [start, end], merge all overlapping intervals and return the minimal set of non-overlapping intervals covering the same ranges. Intervals that only touch at endpoints count as overlapping.
hints: What order makes overlaps easy to detect? Sort by start.
Keep a 'current' interval; extend its end or start a new one.
Touching intervals like [1,4],[4,5]: decide merge per the problem's definition.
approach: Sort by start; sweep, merging into the current interval when overlapping.
complexity: Time O(n log n), Space O(1) excluding output

title: Rotate Array
statement: Rotate an array to the right by k steps in place with O(1) extra space. For example, [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] with k=3 becomes [5,6,7,1,2,3,4]. k may be larger than the array length.
hints: Reversing is its own inverse - how can three reverses rotate?
Reverse all, then reverse the first k, then the rest.
Remember k %= n first.
approach: Reduce k modulo n, then apply the triple-reversal trick: reverse the whole array, reverse the first k elements, reverse the rest. Each element lands in its rotated position with O(1) extra space.
pitfalls: Forgetting k %= n (k can exceed n)

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
statement: Given an integer array and an integer k, count the number of contiguous subarrays whose elements sum to exactly k. The array may contain negative numbers, so a sliding window alone is insufficient.
hints: If you knew all prefix sums, when does a subarray sum to k?
prefix[j] - prefix[i] = k  =>  look up (prefix[j] - k) seen before.
Seed the map with {0: 1} for subarrays starting at index 0.
approach: Running prefix sum; add map.get(prefix - k, 0) to the count; then record prefix.

title: Valid Anagram
statement: Given two strings s and t, determine whether t is an anagram of s — that is, whether t can be formed by rearranging exactly the letters of s. Both strings contain only lowercase English letters in the follow-up; solve the general case first.
hints: Anagrams have identical character frequencies.
Count with a 26-array (lowercase) or a hash map for Unicode.
Early exit when lengths differ.
approach: Build frequency counts for s, decrement for t; all zeros (or use Counter).
complexity: Time O(n), Space O(1) for fixed alphabet
pitfalls: Sorting is O(n log n) - fine but slower

title: Group Anagrams
statement: Given an array of strings, group all anagrams together and return the groups in any order. Two strings are anagrams if one can be rearranged into the other. Optimize beyond pairwise comparison.
hints: Anagrams share a canonical key - what could it be?
Sorted string, or a 26-count tuple (avoids O(k log k) sort).
Map key -> list; return the values.
approach: Hash map keyed by character-count tuple; append each string to its group.
pitfalls: Using the sorted string when k is huge

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Length of the longest substring with all distinct characters.
hints: Grow the right edge; when a duplicate appears, jump the left edge past its last occurrence.
A last-seen index map makes the jump O(1).
left = max(left, last_seen[ch] + 1) - never move left backward.
approach: Sliding window with a last-occurrence map; track max window size.
pitfalls: Moving left to last_seen+1 without max() (moves backward)

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
statement: Given a string s, return the longest palindromic substring it contains. A palindrome reads the same forward and backward. If several answers tie, any one is acceptable.
hints: Every palindrome has a center - expand around each of the 2n-1 centers.
Even and odd lengths need separate centers.
Manacher's O(n) exists; expand-around-center O(n^2) is the expected answer.
approach: Expand around every center: for each index (and each gap between indices for even-length palindromes), expand outward while s[l] == s[r] and keep the longest span found. O(n^2) time, O(1) space.

title: Minimum Window Substring
statement: Smallest substring of s containing all characters of t (with frequencies).
hints: Expand right until the window is valid; then shrink left while it stays valid.
Track 'formed' = how many distinct chars meet their required count.
Record the best window during shrinking.
approach: Sliding window with need-counts and a formed counter; shrink greedily.
pitfalls: Shrinking before the window is valid
Not handling duplicate chars in t

title: Valid Parentheses
statement: Determine if a bracket string is valid (properly closed and nested).
hints: Open brackets go on a stack; closers must match the top.
A closer with an empty stack, or leftover opens at the end, means invalid.
Map closer -> opener for clean matching.
approach: Stack scan; push opens, pop-and-check on closers; valid iff stack empty at end.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
statement: Longest substring with same letter after at most k replacements.
hints: In a window, replacements needed = window_size - max_frequency.
Keep the window valid (replacements <= k); max_freq never decreases - why is that OK?
Because we only care about the maximum window seen.
approach: Sliding window tracking max char frequency; shrink when window - maxfreq > k.

title: Encode and Decode Strings
statement: Design an encoding of a string list to a single string and back (strings may contain any chars).
hints: Delimiters can appear in the data - so prefix each string with its length.
Format: '<len>#<string>' repeated; decode by reading the length first.
Why does this handle every edge case?
approach: Length-prefix encoding; decode by parsing '<digits>#', then slicing exactly len chars.
pitfalls: Using a separator character (breaks on data containing it)

title: Reverse Linked List
statement: Reverse a singly linked list. Implement it iteratively first, then recursively, and be able to explain the pointer manipulation and the recursion's base case in an interview.
hints: You need three pointers: prev, curr, and a temp for next.
At each step: save next, flip curr.next to prev, advance.
Recursive: reverse the rest, then fix the two links at the front.
approach: Iterative three-pointer loop; recursive trust-the-subproblem.
complexity: Time O(n), Space O(1) iterative / O(n) recursive
pitfalls: Losing the next pointer before flipping

title: Linked List Cycle II (find cycle start)
statement: Detect whether a linked list has a cycle; if so return the node where it begins.
hints: Floyd: slow (+1) and fast (+2); meeting means a cycle.
Why does resetting one pointer to head and advancing both find the entrance?
Distance math: they meet k steps before the entrance along the cycle.
approach: Phase 1 meet; phase 2 reset slow to head, advance both one step - meeting node is the entrance.
pitfalls: Returning the meeting point as the answer (wrong)
Hash set works but uses O(n) space

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
statement: Merge two sorted singly linked lists into a single sorted linked list, reusing the existing nodes (no new allocations except a dummy head). Return the head of the merged list.
hints: A dummy head removes the special case for the first node.
Always attach the smaller head and advance it.
Recursive version is a clean 5-liner.
approach: Iterative merge with a dummy head: repeatedly attach the smaller of the two current nodes and advance it. Equivalently, recurse: the merged head is min(l1, l2) with its next set to the merge of the remainders.

title: Remove Nth Node From End
statement: Remove the nth node from the end of a singly linked list in a single pass. For example, removing the 2nd node from the end of 1->2->3->4->5 yields 1->2->3->5. Handle the head-removal edge case.
hints: Two pointers n apart: when the front hits the end, the back is at the target's predecessor.
A dummy head handles n == length (removing the head).
Count the gap carefully: front starts n steps ahead.
approach: Dummy head; advance fast n+1 steps; move both; delete slow.next.
pitfalls: Crash when removing the head without dummy

title: Reorder List
statement: Reorder a list L0 -> L1 -> ... -> Ln-1 -> Ln into L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 -> L2 -> Ln-2 -> ... in place, without changing node values. You may not use extra lists proportional to n.
hints: Split the list in half (slow/fast).
Reverse the second half.
Merge the two halves alternately.
approach: Three composed subproblems, all O(1) space: find the middle with slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half, then zip-merge the two halves alternately.
pitfalls: Wrong split point on odd lengths

title: Add Two Numbers
statement: Two numbers as reverse-order linked lists; return their sum as a list.
hints: Add digit by digit with a carry, like grade-school addition.
Lists may differ in length; a final carry may add a node.
Dummy head again simplifies everything.
approach: Walk both lists with carry; append (total % 10); carry = total // 10.
complexity: Time O(max(n,m)), Space O(max(n,m)) for output

title: Copy List with Random Pointer
statement: Deep-copy a list where each node has next and random pointers.
hints: A map from old node to new node solves it in two passes.
Can you do O(1) space? Interleave copies: A->A'->B->B'.
Then wire A'.random = A.random.next, and finally split the lists.
approach: Hash-map version for clarity; interleave trick for O(1) space.
complexity: Time O(n), Space O(n) map / O(1) interleave
pitfalls: Breaking the original list during split

title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
statement: Reverse the list k nodes at a time; leave the remainder as-is.
hints: Process group by group: reverse k, connect to the next group's result.
First check that k nodes remain; if not, leave them.
Recursion handles 'the rest' elegantly.
approach: Count k nodes; reverse the group; recurse on the remainder; stitch.

title: Palindrome Linked List
statement: Determine if a singly linked list is a palindrome, O(1) space.
hints: Find the middle, reverse the second half, compare.
O(n) space via array copy is the easy version - then optimize.
Optionally restore the list afterward.
approach: Check palindrome in O(1) space: find the middle via slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half in place, then compare the two halves pairwise. Optionally restore the list afterward.

title: Merge K Sorted Lists
statement: Merge k sorted linked lists into one sorted list and return its head. A naive pairwise merge is too slow for large k — find the optimal strategy and analyze its complexity.
hints: Merging pairwise is O(kN); a heap of k heads is better.
Push all heads; repeatedly pop min, push its next.
Divide-and-conquer merging is an O(N log k) alternative.
approach: Min-heap over the current heads of the k lists: repeatedly pop the smallest head, append it to the result, and push that list's next node. Each of the n nodes costs O(log k), for O(n log k) total.
complexity: Time O(N log k), Space O(k)
pitfalls: Forgetting to push next after pop

title: Min Stack
statement: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element, all in O(1) time. The challenge is getMin: think about what auxiliary information must be maintained on each push.
hints: Each stack entry can remember the minimum below it.
Store pairs (value, min_so_far), or keep a parallel min-stack.
Duplicate minimums must be handled - think about pop logic.
approach: Auxiliary min tracking per element; getMin reads the top's stored min.
complexity: Time O(1) all ops, Space O(n)
pitfalls: Popping the min tracking on duplicate mins

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
statement: Evaluate an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation.
hints: Numbers go on the stack; operators pop two operands.
Order matters for - and /: second-popped is the left operand.
Integer division truncates toward zero.
approach: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation with a stack: scan tokens left to right, pushing numbers; on an operator, pop the top two values, apply the operator (careful with operand order for - and /), and push the result.

title: Daily Temperatures
statement: For each day, how many days until a warmer temperature (0 if none).
hints: A decreasing stack of indices holds days awaiting a warmer day.
When today is warmer than the stack top, resolve those days: answer = i - idx.
Each index is pushed and popped once.
approach: Monotonic decreasing stack of indices: for each day, pop all indices with smaller temperatures — the current day is their next warmer day — then push the current index. Each index is pushed and popped once: O(n).
pitfalls: Using temperatures instead of indices (need distances)

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
statement: Given an array of bar heights in a histogram, find the area of the largest rectangle that can be formed within the bars. The brute force is O(n^2); find the linear-time stack solution.
hints: A bar's max rectangle extends until a smaller bar on each side.
Increasing stack: when a smaller bar arrives, pop and compute areas.
A sentinel zero bar flushes the stack at the end.
approach: Monotonic increasing stack with sentinel; area = height * width on pop.
pitfalls: Width miscalculation (use current index - stack top - 1)

title: Valid Parentheses (extended: minimum removals)
statement: Given a bracket string, remove the minimum brackets to make it valid.
hints: First pass: mark indices of unmatched closers and leftover opens.
A stack of indices (not chars) makes marking easy.
Rebuild the string skipping marked indices.
approach: Use an index stack to find unmatched brackets: push indices of '(' and mark matched pairs; positions never matched are the ones to remove. Filter them out in a second pass.

title: Implement Queue using Stacks
statement: Implement a FIFO queue using only two LIFO stacks. The amortized cost of each operation should be O(1). Explain why the amortized bound holds.
hints: One stack for input, one for output; transfer lazily.
Only move elements when the output stack is empty - why?
Amortized O(1): each element moves at most twice.
approach: Two-stack queue: push onto the in-stack; for pop/peek, if the out-stack is empty, transfer everything from the in-stack (reversing order), then serve from the out-stack. Each element moves at most twice: amortized O(1).

title: Next Greater Element I
statement: For each element in nums1, find its next greater element in nums2 (nums1 subset of nums2).
hints: Process nums2 once with a decreasing stack, recording next-greater in a map.
Then answer each nums1 query by lookup.
Remaining stack elements map to -1.
approach: Monotonic stack over nums2 to compute each element's next greater element in one pass, storing results in a map; then answer each query in O(1) by lookup.

title: Asteroid Collision
statement: Asteroids move left/right; simulate collisions (larger survives; equal both explode).
hints: Only right-moving asteroids on the stack can collide with an incoming left-mover.
While loop: resolve repeated collisions against the stack top.
Left-movers never collide with each other.
approach: Stack of right-movers; resolve each left-mover against the stack.
pitfalls: Single if instead of while (chain collisions)

title: Simplify Path (Unix)
statement: Given an absolute Unix-style path, canonicalize it: resolve '.' and '..' components, collapse multiple slashes, and return the simplified canonical path. For example, '/a/./b/../../c/' becomes '/c'.
hints: Split on '/'; push normal names, pop on '..', ignore '.' and empties.
Join the stack with '/' and prefix '/'.
Multiple slashes collapse naturally via the split.
approach: Stack of path components; handle '..', '.', and empty tokens.

title: Decode String (k[encoded])
statement: Decode an encoded string with the pattern k[encoded_string], where the encoded string inside the brackets is repeated exactly k times. Nesting is allowed: '3[a2[c]]' decodes to 'accaccacc'. k is a positive integer.
hints: Two stacks: counts and current strings; '[' pushes, ']' resolves.
Multi-digit counts need accumulation before '['.
Recursive descent is equally clean.
approach: Stack-based parse; on ']' pop count and string, repeat and append.

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
statement: Find the maximum depth (longest root-to-leaf path) of a binary tree.
hints: Depth = 1 + max(depth of children).
Base case: null node has depth 0.
BFS level-counting works too.
approach: Recursive: 1 + max(left, right); or iterative BFS counting levels.

title: Invert Binary Tree
statement: Invert a binary tree: transform it into its mirror image, swapping every node's left and right children. Solve it both recursively and iteratively and compare the approaches.
hints: At each node, swap left and right children.
Then recurse into both (now-swapped) children.
BFS version: swap as you visit each node.
approach: Post-order swap at every node: recursively invert the left and right subtrees, then swap the node's own children. The iterative version uses a stack or queue to visit every node and swap its children.
pitfalls: Swapping after recursing into the wrong child

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
statement: Given a binary tree, find the length (in edges) of the longest path between any two nodes. The path need not pass through the root. This is the tree's diameter.
hints: The longest path through a node = left depth + right depth.
Compute depths bottom-up, tracking the max path seen.
Similar to max-depth, with one extra global.
approach: Post-order traversal returning subtree depth: at each node, the longest path through it is left_depth + right_depth; update a global maximum with this value and return 1 + max(left, right) upward.
pitfalls: Returning the path instead of its length

title: Balanced Binary Tree
statement: Determine if a binary tree is height-balanced (children's heights differ by at most 1 everywhere).
hints: Naive: check balance at each node with depth calls - O(n^2).
Better: return -1 for unbalanced subtrees in one pass.
Combine depth computation with the balance check.
approach: Post-order traversal returning height, or -1 as an unbalanced sentinel: if either subtree returns -1, or their heights differ by more than 1, propagate -1 immediately for early exit.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
statement: Determine whether a binary tree is a valid binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree must be strictly less than the node's value, and all values in its right subtree strictly greater.
hints: Each node must lie within (low, high) bounds passed down.
Inorder traversal of a BST is sorted - alternative check.
Duplicates: decide strict vs non-strict per the problem.
approach: DFS carrying valid bounds: each node must lie within (low, high) inherited from its ancestors; recurse left with high = node.val and right with low = node.val. Alternatively, an inorder traversal must yield strictly increasing values.
pitfalls: Only comparing with parent (grandparent violations missed)

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
statement: Given a binary search tree, find the kth smallest value among its nodes. Do better than a full sort; consider what an inorder traversal gives you and how to stop early.
hints: Inorder traversal visits nodes in sorted order - stop at k.
Iterative with an explicit stack avoids recursion depth issues.
Augmented subtree sizes give O(h) per query.
approach: Inorder traversal visits BST nodes in sorted order: count nodes as you go and stop at the kth. For repeated queries, augment each node with its subtree size (order-statistic tree) for O(log n) per query.
pitfalls: Full traversal when early stop suffices

title: Lowest Common Ancestor (Binary Tree)
statement: Find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a binary tree.
hints: If a subtree contains both/neither/one, what should it return?
Return p or q when found; the first node receiving both is the LCA.
BST version is simpler: walk down by comparisons.
approach: Recursive: combine left/right results; LCA is where both sides are non-null.
pitfalls: Assuming BST properties in a general tree

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
statement: Given a binary tree, return its node values grouped by depth level, from the root level down. For example, levels of [3,9,20,null,null,15,7] are [[3],[9,20],[15,7]].
hints: BFS; capture queue size at each level to group nodes.
DFS with a depth parameter also works (append to level list).
Zigzag: alternate the append direction per level.
approach: Queue-based BFS with per-level snapshots: process the queue level by level, recording each level's values before moving to the next. The queue size at each step is the level width.

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
statement: Design an algorithm to serialize a binary tree to a string and back.
hints: Preorder with '#' markers for nulls captures the full structure.
Deserialize by consuming tokens with an index pointer.
Level-order also works; compare compactness.
approach: Preorder encode with null markers; recursive decode consuming tokens.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
statement: Find the maximum path sum in a binary tree, where a path is any sequence of nodes connected by parent-child edges and may start and end at any nodes. Node values may be negative.
hints: For each node: best downward path = val + max(0, left, right).
A path THROUGH the node can use both children: candidate = val + left + right.
Return downward-best upward; track the global through-max.
approach: Post-order returning max downward path; global max over through-paths.
pitfalls: Confusing return value with global answer

title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
statement: Count nodes where the path from root contains no greater value.
hints: Pass the maximum seen so far down the recursion.
A node is good iff node.val >= max_so_far.
Update max_so_far for children.
approach: DFS carrying the maximum value seen on the path from the root: count the node when node.val >= path max, then recurse with the updated maximum. Each root-to-leaf path is examined once.
pitfalls: Using global max instead of path max

title: Construct Tree from Preorder and Inorder
statement: Rebuild a binary tree from its preorder and inorder traversals.
hints: preorder[0] is the root; find it in inorder to split left/right subtrees.
A value->index map makes the split O(1).
Recurse with index ranges, not slices (avoid O(n^2) copying).
approach: Recursive build with (pre_idx, in_left, in_right) ranges and an index map.
pitfalls: Linear search for root in inorder

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
statement: Find the kth largest element in an unsorted array without fully sorting it. Compare the heap-based approach with the selection-algorithm approach and their trade-offs.
hints: A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest; the top is the answer.
Quickselect partitions like quicksort: average O(n).
Compare: heap is simpler, quickselect is faster on average.
approach: Maintain a min-heap of size k while scanning: push each element and pop when the heap exceeds k. The heap top is the kth largest. Quickselect gives average O(n) as an alternative.
complexity: Time O(n log k) heap / O(n) avg quickselect, Space O(k)

title: Top K Frequent Elements
statement: Given an integer array, return the k most frequent elements. Your algorithm's time complexity should be better than O(n log n) — think about which data structures combine well here.
hints: Count frequencies, then either heap (O(n log k)) or bucket by count (O(n)).
Bucket index = frequency; scan buckets from high to low.
Which is better depends on constraints - discuss.
approach: Build a frequency map, then bucket-sort elements by count (buckets indexed by frequency) and collect from the highest buckets; equivalently, keep a min-heap of size k keyed by frequency.
pitfalls: Sorting all frequencies O(n log n)
Forgetting ties can exceed k (fine - return any k)

title: Find Median from Data Stream
statement: Design a data structure supporting addNum (insert a number from a stream) and findMedian (return the median of all numbers seen so far). Both operations should be efficient for a long stream.
hints: Two heaps: max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper half.
Keep sizes balanced (differ by at most 1); median from the tops.
Every addNum: push, then rebalance.
approach: Dual-heap with size invariant: a max-heap holds the lower half, a min-heap the upper half, with sizes differing by at most one. The median is the top of the larger heap (or the average of both tops).
complexity: Time O(log n) add, O(1) median; Space O(n)
pitfalls: Python heapq is min-heap: negate for max-heap

title: Task Scheduler
statement: Minimum intervals to run tasks with cooldown n between same tasks.
hints: The most frequent task dictates the skeleton: (maxFreq-1) * (n+1) slots.
Add the count of tasks tied for max frequency.
Take max with total tasks (no idle needed if dense).
approach: Frequency formula; or greedy simulation with max-heap + cooldown queue.

title: K Closest Points to Origin
statement: Given an array of points in the plane, return the k points closest to the origin (0, 0). Avoid computing all distances and fully sorting when k is much smaller than n.
hints: Compare squared distances (skip sqrt).
Max-heap of size k, or quickselect on distance.
Sorting all is O(n log n) - beatable.
approach: Keep a max-heap of size k keyed by squared distance from the origin: for each point, push it and pop the farthest when the heap exceeds k. Quickselect on distances is the average-O(n) alternative.
complexity: Time O(n log k), Space O(k)

title: IPO (maximize capital with k projects)
statement: Pick up to k projects to maximize final capital; each needs min capital and yields profit.
hints: Sort projects by required capital; use a max-heap for affordable profits.
Each round: move newly-affordable projects into the heap, take the best.
Greedy works because profits only increase affordability.
approach: Sort projects by required capital, then run k rounds: push every newly affordable project's profit into a max-heap and take the largest. This greedily maximizes capital after k investments.
complexity: Time O(n log n), Space O(n)
pitfalls: Re-scanning affordable projects each round O(kn)
Taking projects in requirement order only

title: Sliding Window Maximum
statement: Given an integer array and a window size k, return the maximum value in each sliding window of size k as it moves from left to right. Achieve O(n) time.
hints: A decreasing deque of indices gives O(n): front is always the max.
Evict indices outside the window from the front.
Heap with lazy deletion is O(n log k) - acceptable alternative.
approach: Monotonic deque; maintain decreasing values, drop out-of-window.
pitfalls: Heap without lazy deletion of stale entries

title: Meeting Rooms II (min conference rooms)
statement: Given an array of meeting time intervals [start, end), find the minimum number of conference rooms required so that all meetings can be held without overlap in the same room.
hints: Sort by start; a min-heap of end times tracks busy rooms.
If the earliest-ending room frees before this starts, reuse it.
Heap size at the end = answer.
approach: Sort meetings by start time and sweep through them, keeping a min-heap of end times for rooms currently in use. For each meeting, free every room whose meeting has ended (heap top <= start), then push the current meeting's end time. The heap's maximum size is the answer.
complexity: Time O(n log n), Space O(n)

title: Number of Islands
statement: Count the islands (connected '1's, 4-directional) in a binary grid.
hints: Each unvisited '1' starts a new island - flood-fill it.
Mark visited by flipping to '0' (in-place) or a visited set.
DFS recursive or BFS iterative both work.
approach: Scan grid; on unvisited '1', increment count and flood-fill its region.
complexity: Time O(mn), Space O(mn) worst-case recursion

title: Clone Graph
statement: Deep-copy a connected undirected graph given a reference node.
hints: A map from original node to clone handles cycles.
DFS: clone node, then recursively clone neighbors.
BFS version is equally valid.
approach: DFS/BFS clone with an old->new node map: when visiting a node, create its clone once, then wire each neighbor's clone (creating recursively as needed). The map prevents infinite loops on cycles.
pitfalls: Infinite recursion on cycles (no map check)

title: Course Schedule
statement: There are n courses labeled 0..n-1 with prerequisite pairs [course, prerequisite]. Determine whether it is possible to finish all courses — equivalently, whether the prerequisite graph has a cycle.
hints: Model as a directed graph; the question is cycle detection.
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove zero-indegree nodes.
If all nodes are removed, no cycle exists.
approach: Build adjacency + indegree; BFS from zero-indegree nodes; check count.
pitfalls: DFS color method: forgetting the 'visiting' state

title: Course Schedule II (return ordering)
statement: Given course prerequisites as [course, prerequisite] pairs, return a valid order in which to take all n courses, or an empty array if no such order exists (i.e., the graph has a cycle).
hints: Same as Course Schedule, but record the removal order.
That order IS a valid topological ordering.
Any valid order is accepted.
approach: Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove nodes with zero indegree, recording the dequeue order. If every node is dequeued, the recorded order is a valid topological ordering; otherwise a cycle exists.
pitfalls: Returning partial order on cycle (must return [])

title: Rotting Oranges
statement: Minutes until no fresh orange remains (4-directional spread per minute); -1 if impossible.
hints: Multi-source BFS: enqueue ALL rotten oranges at time 0.
Level-order traversal counts minutes.
Count fresh oranges; leftovers mean -1.
approach: BFS from all rotten sources simultaneously; levels = minutes.
pitfalls: BFS from each rotten separately (wrong timing)

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
statement: Cells with heights; find cells from which water flows to both oceans (borders).
hints: Forward simulation from every cell is O((mn)^2) - reverse it.
Start BFS/DFS from each ocean's border, moving to equal-or-higher cells.
Intersect the two reachable sets.
approach: Two reverse flood-fills from ocean borders; intersect reachable cells.
pitfalls: Wrong flow direction (must go uphill in reverse)

title: Graph Valid Tree
statement: Given n nodes and edges, determine if they form a valid tree.
hints: A tree: exactly n-1 edges AND connected (either implies the other given no self-loops... check both).
Union-Find: any union of already-connected nodes means a cycle.
Or DFS: no cycles and visit count == n.
approach: A connected undirected graph with n nodes is a tree iff it has exactly n-1 edges and no cycles. Check the edge count first, then use Union-Find to detect any cycle or disconnected component.

title: Number of Connected Components
statement: Given n nodes labeled 0..n-1 and a list of undirected edges, count the number of connected components in the graph. Consider both DFS and union-find solutions.
hints: Union all edges; count distinct roots.
Or DFS/BFS from each unvisited node, counting launches.
Isolated nodes count as their own component.
approach: Union-Find over all edges: union the endpoints of each edge, then count distinct parents. Each distinct set is one connected component. Path compression keeps it nearly linear.

title: Word Ladder
statement: Shortest transformation sequence length from beginWord to endWord, changing one letter at a time through valid words.
hints: Model words as a graph; BFS gives the shortest path.
Neighbors via wildcard patterns (*ot -> hot, dot) precomputed in a map.
Bidirectional BFS halves the search.
approach: BFS over word ladders using pattern buckets: map patterns like 'h*t' to all matching words for O(1) neighbor lookup. Bidirectional BFS from both ends roughly halves the explored space.
complexity: Time O(n * L^2), Space O(n * L)
pitfalls: Rebuilding neighbors by scanning all words each time

title: Network Delay Time (Dijkstra)
statement: Time for a signal from node k to reach all nodes (directed weighted edges); -1 if unreachable.
hints: Classic single-source shortest path with non-negative weights: Dijkstra.
Heap of (dist, node); relax edges; skip stale entries.
Answer = max distance; unreachable nodes -> -1.
approach: Run Dijkstra's algorithm from node k to get shortest times to all nodes. The answer is the maximum of these distances; if any node is unreachable, return -1. A binary heap keeps it O(E log V).
complexity: Time O(e log n), Space O(n+e)

title: Alien Dictionary
statement: Derive the character order from a list of words sorted in an alien language.
hints: Compare adjacent words; first differing chars give an ordering edge.
Watch the invalid case: 'abc' before 'ab' is impossible.
Topological sort; a cycle means no valid order.
approach: Build graph from adjacent pairs; Kahn's sort; validate prefix case.

title: Redundant Connection
statement: A tree plus one extra edge; return the edge that can be removed to restore the tree.
hints: Process edges in order; the first edge joining two connected nodes is redundant.
Return the LAST such edge per the problem statement (with plain union-find it's the first found - re-read the spec).
Actually: return the edge that appears last in input among cycle-forming edges.
approach: Union-Find in input order; track the last cycle-forming edge.
pitfalls: Returning the first cycle edge instead of the last

title: Climbing Stairs
statement: You are climbing a staircase with n steps; each move you may climb 1 or 2 steps. Count the number of distinct ways to reach the top. Recognize the recurrence before coding.
hints: Ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2): the last step is 1 or 2.
It's Fibonacci; two variables suffice.
Base: ways(1)=1, ways(2)=2.
approach: Iterative Fibonacci with O(1) space: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), since the last step is 1 or 2. Keep only the previous two values and roll forward; handle n = 0 and n = 1 as base cases.

title: House Robber
statement: A robber wants to rob houses arranged in a line; robbing two adjacent houses triggers an alarm. Given each house's loot value, compute the maximum loot possible without triggering the alarm.
hints: At each house: rob it (plus dp[i-2]) or skip it (dp[i-1]).
Two variables rolling forward.
Circular street: run twice, excluding first or last.
approach: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]): either skip house i or rob it plus the best up to i-2. Iterate once keeping two variables, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.

title: Coin Change
statement: Given coin denominations and a target amount, find the fewest coins needed to make up that amount; return -1 if it is impossible. You may use each denomination any number of times.
hints: dp[x] = 1 + min(dp[x - coin]) over coins; INF if unreachable.
Iterate amounts outer, coins inner (for min-coins formulation).
Greedy fails: coins [1,3,4], amount 6 -> greedy gives 4+1+1, optimal 3+3.
approach: Bottom-up DP over amounts with an INF sentinel: dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - coin]) over all coins <= a. dp[0] = 0; any amount still INF at the end is unreachable, so return -1.
pitfalls: Wrong loop order confusion with counting variant

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
statement: Given an integer array, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. The subsequence need not be contiguous. Improve on the O(n^2) DP if you can.
hints: O(n^2): dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) for j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].
O(n log n): maintain tails[]; binary-search each number's position.
Tails isn't the subsequence - only its length is correct.
approach: Patience sorting with binary search on the tails array: tails[i] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length i+1. For each x, binary-search its position in tails. O(n log n).
complexity: Time O(n log n), Space O(n)

title: Word Break
statement: Given a string s and a dictionary of words, determine whether s can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words. The same word may be reused.
hints: dp[i]: prefix of length i is segmentable.
For each i, try every j < i where dp[j] and s[j:i] in dict.
BFS/DFS with memo is equivalent.
approach: DP over prefix lengths: dp[i] is true if s[:i] can be segmented. For each i, try every split j < i with dp[j] true and s[j:i] in the dictionary (use a set for O(1) lookup).

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
statement: Given an integer array, determine whether it can be partitioned into two subsets with equal sum. Reduce this to a known knapsack-style decision problem.
hints: Total must be even; then it's subset-sum to total/2.
1D boolean DP iterating sums BACKWARD (avoid reuse).
Classic 0/1 knapsack.
approach: Backward-iterating boolean DP for subset sum: dp[s] tracks achievable sums; for each number, iterate s downward so each number is used once. Answer is dp[target] where target = total // 2 (total must be even).

title: Decode Ways
statement: A message is encoded by mapping 1->'A', 2->'B', ..., 26->'Z'. Given a digit string, count how many ways it can be decoded. Watch out for '0', which cannot stand alone.
hints: dp[i] += dp[i-1] if s[i-1] != '0'; dp[i] += dp[i-2] if 10 <= two-digit <= 26.
'0' is the trap: valid only inside 10 or 20.
Leading zeros make the answer 0 immediately.
approach: Linear DP over the string: dp[i] counts decodings of the first i characters. From position i you may take one digit (1-9) or two digits (10-26); a '0' can only be consumed as part of 10 or 20. Sum the valid transitions.

title: Unique Paths with Obstacles
statement: Count paths from top-left to bottom-right moving only down/right, avoiding obstacles.
hints: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]; obstacles force 0.
First row/col: 1s until the first obstacle.
In-place on the grid is fine.
approach: Grid DP with obstacle zeroing: dp[i][j] = 0 if the cell is an obstacle, else dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1]; seed the first row and column carefully since a single obstacle blocks the whole line.

title: Edit Distance
statement: Minimum operations (insert, delete, replace) to convert word1 to word2.
hints: Define dp[i][j] on prefixes; consider the last characters.
If equal: dp[i-1][j-1]; else 1 + min(delete, insert, replace).
Base: converting to/from empty string costs the length.
approach: 2D DP over prefix pairs with the three-operation recurrence: dp[i][j] = min(delete, insert, replace) derived from dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1], with dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] when the characters match.
pitfalls: Forgetting replace as a distinct op

title: Longest Common Subsequence
statement: Given two strings, find the length of their longest common subsequence — the longest sequence that appears as a subsequence (not necessarily contiguous) in both strings.
hints: Match -> 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]; else max of skipping one char from either.
Backtrack through the table to reconstruct it.
Subsequence, not substring: gaps allowed.
approach: Classic 2D DP: dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i and first j characters; match extends dp[i-1][j-1] by one, mismatch takes max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). An optional reconstruction pass recovers the actual subsequence.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
statement: Given an integer array, find the contiguous subarray with the largest product and return that product. Negative numbers make this trickier than the maximum-sum variant.
hints: Negatives flip: track BOTH max and min ending at each position.
On a negative, swap max and min before multiplying.
Kadane alone fails - why?
approach: Rolling max_ending/min_ending with a swap on negatives: a negative x turns the smallest product into the largest, so swap the two trackers before updating. Track the global best across the scan.
pitfalls: Only tracking max (sign flips break it)

title: Jump Game II (min jumps)
statement: Minimum jumps to reach the end (each element = max jump length).
hints: Greedy layers: current jump's reach vs the farthest reachable.
When you exhaust the current range, jump and extend.
BFS-level thinking on an implicit graph.
approach: Greedy range expansion: track how far you can reach with the current number of jumps, and extend the farthest reachable point within that range. Each time you exhaust the current range, increment the jump count.

title: Combination Sum
statement: All unique combinations summing to target; candidates reusable.
hints: Backtrack with a start index to avoid duplicate permutations.
Sort first so you can prune when the remainder goes negative.
Variants change the reuse/duplicate rules.
approach: DFS with start-index and pruning: build combinations by choosing each next element from positions after the last chosen one, and prune branches that cannot beat the best solution found so far.
pitfalls: Permutations instead of combinations (no start index)

title: N-Queens II (count)
statement: Count the number of distinct ways to place n queens on an n x n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other. Return the count, not the boards themselves.
hints: Place row by row; track attacked columns and diagonals in sets.
Diagonal ids: r+c and r-c are constant per diagonal.
Bitmask version is the optimized classic.
approach: Backtracking with column/diagonal sets: place queens row by row, tracking occupied columns and the two diagonal families (r+c and r-c) in hash sets for O(1) conflict checks; count complete placements.
pitfalls: Counting symmetric duplicates separately is fine

title: Regular Expression Matching
statement: Match string against pattern with '.' and '*' (zero or more of preceding).
hints: dp(i,j): does s[i:] match p[j:]? Handle '*' by zero-match (skip) or consume-one.
Memoize the recursion; base cases on empty pattern/string.
Draw the decision tree for 'a*' carefully.
approach: Memoized recursion on (i, j) with the star-branching rule: for pattern[j] == '*', either skip the star (match zero chars) or consume s[i] and stay on the star. Memoize (i, j) to avoid exponential blowup.

title: Burst Balloons
statement: Max coins bursting balloons; bursting i yields nums[l]*nums[i]*nums[r].
hints: Think REVERSE: which balloon bursts LAST in interval (l, r)?
dp[l][r] = max over k of dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + nums[l]*nums[k]*nums[r].
Pad with 1s at both ends.
approach: Interval DP over the last-burst choice: for interval [l, r], try bursting each k last, which splits the interval into [l, k-1] and [k+1, r] plus the coins from bursting k with its new neighbors. Memoize on (l, r).

title: Binary Search (classic)
statement: Given a sorted integer array and a target value, return the target's index, or -1 if it is absent. Implement binary search iteratively and handle the midpoint computation safely.
hints: Maintain [lo, hi]; mid = lo + (hi-lo)//2 avoids overflow.
Shrink the half that cannot contain the target.
Loop invariant: target in [lo, hi] if present.
approach: Iterative halving with an overflow-safe midpoint (lo + (hi - lo) // 2): compare nums[mid] with the target and discard the half that cannot contain it. Loop until found or lo > hi.
pitfalls: Infinite loop from wrong bound updates

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: Search for a target value in a rotated sorted array (sorted ascending, then rotated at an unknown pivot) in O(log n) time. Duplicates are not present in the basic version.
hints: One half is always sorted - determine which via nums[lo] <= nums[mid].
Check if the target lies in the sorted half; else go to the other.
Duplicates break the worst case to O(n).
approach: Modified binary search using the sorted-half property: at each step, one half of [lo, hi] is sorted. Check whether the target lies in the sorted half; if yes, search there, else search the other half.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: Find the minimum element in a rotated sorted array in O(log n) time. Think about which half of the array must contain the minimum at each step.
hints: Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi] to decide the side.
The minimum is the only element smaller than its predecessor.
Duplicates: hi -= 1 fallback.
approach: Binary search toward the rotation pivot: compare nums[mid] with nums[right]. If nums[mid] > nums[right], the minimum lies to the right of mid; otherwise it is at mid or to the left. Shrink until lo == hi.

title: Koko Eating Bananas
statement: Minimum integer eating speed k to finish all piles within h hours.
hints: Binary search the ANSWER: speed in [1, max(piles)].
Feasibility: sum(ceil(pile / k)) <= h.
Monotonic: faster speeds only help.
approach: Binary search on the eating speed with a feasibility check: for a candidate speed k, compute total hours as sum(ceil(pile / k)); if it fits within h hours, try a slower speed, else go faster.
complexity: Time O(n log max), Space O(1)

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
statement: Given two sorted arrays, find the median of the combined sorted array in O(log(m+n)) time. The naive merge is O(m+n); the optimal solution partitions both arrays.
hints: Binary search the partition: i + j = (m+n+1)//2 on the smaller array.
Valid when maxLeft1 <= minRight2 and maxLeft2 <= minRight1.
Handle empty partitions with infinities.
approach: Partition binary search: binary-search the split point in the smaller array such that all left elements <= all right elements; the median is then derived from the border values. O(log(min(m, n))).

title: Search a 2D Matrix
statement: Matrix with rows sorted and first-of-row > last-of-previous; search target.
hints: Flatten conceptually: index i -> (i//n, i%n); binary search once.
Or staircase from top-right in O(m+n).
Compare the two approaches.
approach: Binary search on the virtual flat array: treat the m x n matrix as a sorted array of length m*n, mapping flat index i to (i // n, i % n). Standard binary search then applies directly.

title: Find Peak Element
statement: A peak element is strictly greater than its neighbors. Given an array where no two adjacent elements are equal, find any peak in O(log n) time.
hints: If nums[mid] < nums[mid+1], a peak must exist to the right.
The array edges act as -infinity.
Invariant: the chosen half always contains a peak.
approach: Binary search toward the rising slope: compare nums[mid] with nums[mid+1]. If nums[mid] < nums[mid+1], a peak must exist to the right; otherwise one exists at mid or to the left. This halves the range each step.

title: Time Based Key-Value Store
statement: set(key, value, timestamp); get(key, timestamp) returns the latest value at or before timestamp.
hints: Per key, keep a list of (timestamp, value) in increasing order.
Binary search for the rightmost timestamp <= target.
Strictly increasing timestamps simplify appends.
approach: Hash map from value to sorted timestamp list, plus binary search: store (timestamp, value) pairs per key in insertion order (timestamps are increasing), then binary-search the latest timestamp <= query time.
complexity: Time O(log n) get, Space O(n)
pitfalls: Leftmost vs rightmost binary search confusion

title: Sqrt(x) without built-ins
statement: Compute the integer square root of a non-negative integer x: the largest integer r such that r*r <= x. Do not use built-in exponent or root functions; x can be up to 2^31 - 1, so watch for overflow.
hints: Binary search answer in [0, x]; compare mid*mid with x.
Newton's method converges faster - mention it.
Avoid overflow: compare mid <= x // mid.
approach: Binary search on the answer range [0, x]: for mid, compare mid*mid with x using division (mid > x // mid) to avoid overflow. Keep the largest mid with mid*mid <= x.

title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days
statement: Minimum ship capacity to ship all weights within D days (order preserved).
hints: Binary search capacity in [max(weights), sum(weights)].
Feasibility: greedy day-packing count <= D.
Same answer-space pattern as Koko.
approach: Binary search on ship capacity with a greedy feasibility check: for a candidate capacity, count how many days the greedy loading needs; fewer days than allowed means the capacity suffices.
complexity: Time O(n log sum), Space O(1)
pitfalls: Lower bound below max single weight

title: Find First and Last Position in Sorted Array
statement: Find the start/end indices of target in sorted array; [-1,-1] if absent.
hints: Two binary searches: lower bound and upper bound.
Or one search then expand - but that's O(n) worst case.
bisect_left / bisect_right model.
approach: Lower-bound and upper-bound binary searches: find the first index >= target and the first index > target; their difference is the occurrence count, found in O(log n).

title: Split Array Largest Sum
statement: Given an integer array and an integer k, split the array into k contiguous subarrays to minimize the largest sum among the subarrays, and return that minimized largest sum. Binary-search the answer space.
hints: Binary search the answer: largest-sum in [max(nums), sum(nums)].
Feasibility: greedy counting of subarrays needed.
DP O(n^2 k) exists but binary search wins.
approach: Binary search on the minimized maximum with a greedy check: for a candidate limit, greedily cut subarrays whenever the running sum would exceed it, counting pieces; if pieces <= k, the limit is feasible.
complexity: Time O(n log sum), Space O(1)
pitfalls: DP when constraints allow binary search

title: Two Sum (hashmap drill)
statement: Revisit Two Sum focusing on the hashmap pattern's generalizations.
hints: Complement lookup is the core pattern.
Same pattern: pair sums, difference k, subarray sums.
One pass vs two pass trade-offs.
approach: Single-pass complement map: for each x, check whether target - x is already in the map; if yes, return both indices, otherwise store x with its index and continue.

title: Group Anagrams (hashmap drill)
statement: Given an array of strings, group anagrams together using hashing rather than pairwise comparison. Design a hashable canonical key for each anagram class.
hints: Canonical key per string: count-tuple is O(k).
Map key -> list; deterministic and fast.
Prime-product hashing is a fun alternative (overflow caveats).
approach: Count-tuple keys in a hash map: for each string, build the 26-count tuple of its letters as the canonical key (O(L) per string, no sorting), and append the string to the bucket for that key.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
statement: Given an unsorted integer array, find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers in O(n) time. Sorting first would be O(n log n) — avoid it.
hints: Only start counting from sequence beginnings (x-1 not in set).
Each number is then visited at most twice overall.
Sorting is O(n log n) - beat it with a set.
approach: Hash set with expansion only from sequence starts: for each number, if num - 1 is absent from the set, it starts a run — then count upward consecutively. Each number is visited O(1) times amortized.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K (hashmap drill)
statement: Count the number of contiguous subarrays summing to k using prefix sums and a hash map, in O(n) time. Explain why the map stores prefix-sum frequencies.
hints: prefix[j] - prefix[i] = k -> need count of (prefix - k).
Seed {0: 1}; update after querying (order matters).
Works with negatives where sliding window fails.
approach: Running prefix with frequency map: prefix[i] - prefix[j] = k means prefix[j] = prefix[i] - k, so for each new prefix sum, add the stored frequency of (prefix - k) to the answer, then record the prefix.

title: LRU Cache (hashmap + list drill)
statement: Design an LRU cache supporting O(1) get and put with a capacity limit; when the capacity is exceeded, evict the least recently used entry. Combine a hash map with a doubly linked list.
hints: Map key -> node; doubly-linked list for recency order.
Dummy head/tail simplify edge cases.
OrderedDict is the library shortcut - implement manually first.
approach: Hash map plus a doubly linked list with dummy head/tail: the map gives O(1) node access, and moving a node to the front on each access keeps the tail as the eviction candidate.
pitfalls: Singly linked list (can't evict in O(1))
Forgetting to update map on eviction

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
statement: Design a set supporting insert, delete, and getRandom (uniform over current elements), all in amortized O(1) time. The delete operation is the tricky one.
hints: Array for random access + map value -> index.
Delete by swapping with the last element.
Duplicates need index sets.
approach: Array + index map with swap-remove: store values in a list and value->index in a dict. To delete, swap the element with the last one, update the moved element's index, and pop — all O(1).

title: Design HashMap (from scratch)
statement: Implement a hash map from scratch supporting put, get, and remove. Choose a collision strategy, handle resizing, and analyze the amortized complexity.
hints: Buckets array; chaining for collisions.
Hash function: built-in hash % capacity; handle negatives.
Resize when load factor exceeds ~0.75.
approach: Separate chaining with dynamic resize: bucket array of linked lists (or lists); on put, hash to a bucket and update or append. When the load factor exceeds a threshold, double the buckets and rehash everything.

title: Word Pattern (bijection check)
statement: Given a pattern string and a space-separated word string, check whether the pattern bijectively maps to the words — e.g. pattern 'abba' matches 'dog cat cat dog' but not 'dog cat cat fish'.
hints: Bijection needs BOTH directions checked.
Two maps, or one map + one set of used words.
Isomorphic Strings is the twin problem.
approach: Dual-direction mapping validation: build char->word and word->char maps in one pass; the pattern matches iff both maps stay consistent (bijection), which a single map alone cannot guarantee.

title: Reverse Integer (32-bit clamp)
statement: Reverse digits of a 32-bit signed integer; return 0 on overflow.
hints: Build the reversed number digit by digit.
Check overflow BEFORE multiplying: rev > INT_MAX//10 etc.
Python ints don't overflow - simulate the check anyway.
approach: Digit extraction loop with pre-overflow checks: before result = result * 10 + digit, verify result <= (INT_MAX - digit) // 10 so the multiplication can never overflow a 32-bit signed integer.

title: Pow(x, n) (fast exponentiation)
statement: Compute x raised to the power n in O(log n) time, where n may be negative. Handle the n = -2^31 edge case without overflow.
hints: x^n = (x^2)^(n/2); handle odd n with an extra multiply.
Negative n: invert x first.
Iterative bit-loop version too.
approach: Binary exponentiation, recursive or iterative: x^n = (x^2)^(n/2) when n is even, x * x^(n-1) when odd. Handle negative n by inverting x, and compute n = -2^31 via long to avoid overflow.
complexity: Time O(log n), Space O(log n) / O(1)

title: Spiral Matrix
statement: Given an m x n matrix, return all its elements in spiral order, starting at the top-left and moving clockwise inward.
hints: Shrink boundaries: top, bottom, left, right.
After each wall, check the loop condition again (single row/col left).
Direction arrays are an alternative.
approach: Boundary-shrinking traversal: maintain top/bottom/left/right edges and walk the perimeter inward, tightening the boundary after each side so corners are never visited twice.
complexity: Time O(mn), Space O(1) excluding output

title: Rotate Image (90 degrees in place)
statement: Rotate an n x n matrix 90 degrees clockwise in place, using O(1) extra space. Find the two-step decomposition that makes this easy.
hints: Transpose then reverse each row - two clean steps.
Or rotate 4-cycles layer by layer.
Verify on 3x3 by hand.
approach: Rotate in place via transpose + row reversal: first swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for j > i, then reverse every row.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes (O(1) space)
statement: Given an m x n matrix, if any cell is zero, set its entire row and column to zero — using only constant extra space. The first row/column can serve as marker storage with care.
hints: Use the first row and column as marker storage.
Two flags remember whether the first row/col themselves need zeroing.
Mark first, then zero in a second pass.
approach: Use the first row and column as markers for which rows/cols contain zeros, with two boolean flags remembering whether the first row/col themselves need zeroing; then zero in a second pass.

title: Game of Life (in-place)
statement: Compute the next state of Conway's Game of Life on a grid in place: each cell's next state depends on its eight neighbors' current states, so the update must not clobber data still needed.
hints: Encode transitions in extra bits: 2 = dead->alive, 3 = alive->dead.
Count live neighbors using val % 2 (original state).
Second pass: shift right to finalize.
approach: In-place state encoding with bit tricks: store the next state in a second bit of each cell (e.g. bit 1), computing all next states from bit 0 first, then shift every cell right by one.
pitfalls: Counting transitional states as live/dead wrong

title: String to Integer (atoi)
statement: Implement atoi: parse a string to a 32-bit signed integer, skipping leading whitespace, handling an optional sign, stopping at the first non-digit, and clamping overflow to [-2^31, 2^31 - 1].
hints: Skip whitespace, read optional sign, then digits.
Clamp on overflow DURING parsing (pre-check).
Stop at the first non-digit.
approach: State-machine parse with overflow pre-checks: skip whitespace, read the optional sign, then accumulate digits while checking result > (INT_MAX - digit) // 10 before each step, clamping on overflow.

title: Integer to Roman / Roman to Integer
statement: Convert integers to Roman numerals and Roman numerals back to integers, handling subtractive notation (IV = 4, IX = 9, XL = 40, etc.) correctly in both directions.
hints: Greedy subtraction with value-symbol pairs including 4/9 forms (IV, IX...).
Reverse: add, but subtract when a smaller precedes a larger.
Table-driven is cleanest.
approach: Greedy table mapping both directions: for int->Roman, repeatedly subtract the largest fitting denomination from a value-symbol table including subtractive pairs; for Roman->int, add values but subtract twice when a smaller numeral precedes a larger one.

title: Multiply Strings (big integers as strings)
statement: Multiply two non-negative integer strings without big-int libs.
hints: Grade-school multiplication: result[i+j] += d1*d2, then carry.
Result has at most m+n digits.
Strip leading zeros.
approach: Positional accumulation plus a carry pass: sum each digit position across all numbers, then sweep right-to-left propagating carries (digit = total % 10, carry = total // 10).

title: Plus One (digit array)
statement: Given a non-empty array of digits representing a large non-negative integer, increment it by one and return the resulting digit array. Handle the all-9s carry case.
hints: Add from the right with carry; early exit when no carry.
All 9s -> need a new leading 1.
The easy version of big-integer handling.
approach: Right-to-left increment with carry: add one to the last digit and propagate the carry leftward; if the carry survives past the most significant digit, prepend a 1 (the all-9s case).

title: Happy Number (cycle detection)
statement: Determine whether a number is 'happy': repeatedly replace it by the sum of the squares of its digits; if the process reaches 1 it is happy, if it loops forever it is not. Detect the loop efficiently.
hints: The sequence either reaches 1 or cycles - detect the cycle.
Floyd or a seen-set both work.
Why must it cycle? Values stay bounded.
approach: Cycle detection on the digit-square iteration: the process either reaches 1 or enters the known unhappy cycle, so track seen values in a set (or use slow/fast pointers) and stop when a value repeats.
complexity: Time O(log n) per step, Space O(1) Floyd

title: Excel Sheet Column Title/Number
statement: Convert between 1-indexed column numbers and titles (A..Z, AA...).
hints: It's base-26 but 1-indexed: no zero digit.
Number->title: (n-1) % 26 + 'A', then (n-1)//26.
Title->number: standard base-26 accumulation.
approach: Adjusted base-26 conversion both ways: Excel columns are 1-indexed base-26 with no zero digit, so decrement before each divmod step when encoding, and accumulate digit*26^pos with A=1 when decoding.
pitfalls: Plain base-26 (off by one on Z->AA)

title: Flood Fill
statement: An image is represented by an m x n integer grid where each value is a pixel color. Given a starting pixel (sr, sc) and a new color, perform a flood fill: change the starting pixel and all 4-directionally connected pixels of the same original color to the new color, then return the modified image. If the new color equals the original color, return the image unchanged.
hints: This is a graph traversal where each pixel is a node connected to its 4 neighbors.
Only spread to neighbors that still have the ORIGINAL color — capture it before you start.
Handle the edge case where the new color equals the original color to avoid infinite recursion.
approach: Capture the original color at (sr, sc); if it equals the new color, return the image as-is. Otherwise DFS/BFS from the start: paint the current pixel, then recurse into 4-directional neighbors that still have the original color. Each pixel is painted once, giving O(m*n) time and O(m*n) worst-case recursion space.
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(m*n) worst case (recursion stack / queue).
pitfalls: Forgetting the same-color early return causes infinite recursion.
Using 8-directional connectivity when the problem specifies 4-directional.
Comparing against the new color instead of the captured original color during spread.

title: Find if Path Exists in Graph
statement: There is a bi-directional graph with n vertices labeled 0 to n-1 and a list of undirected edges. Given a source vertex and a destination vertex, determine whether a valid path exists between them. Return true if they are connected, false otherwise.
hints: Build an adjacency list from the edge list first.
Any graph traversal (BFS or DFS) from the source answers this — stop early when you reach the destination.
A visited set prevents revisiting nodes and infinite loops on cycles.
approach: Build an adjacency list, then BFS/DFS from source with a visited set. Return true the moment the destination is dequeled/visited; if the traversal exhausts without reaching it, return false. Runs in O(n + e) time and space.
complexity: Time O(n + e), space O(n + e) for the adjacency list and visited set.
pitfalls: Treating edges as directed when they are bi-directional.
Missing the trivial case where source equals destination (path of length 0 exists).
Rebuilding the adjacency list per query instead of once.

title: Number of Islands (Easy Intro)
statement: Given an m x n binary grid where '1' represents land and '0' water, count the number of islands. An island is a group of '1's connected 4-directionally, surrounded by water. Assume the grid border is surrounded by water. Solve it by sinking each discovered island with DFS.
hints: Scan every cell; each time you find an unvisited '1', you have found a new island.
From that cell, DFS outward and flip every connected '1' to '0' so it is never counted again.
The answer is simply how many times you started a fresh DFS.
approach: Iterate over all cells; when grid[i][j] == '1', increment the count and launch a DFS that flips the entire connected component to '0' (marking visited in place). Each cell is flipped at most once: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) worst-case stack space, O(1) extra space besides the recursion.
complexity: Time O(m*n), space O(m*n) worst-case recursion depth.
pitfalls: Counting the same island twice by not marking visited cells.
Stack overflow on huge grids — consider iterative BFS for production.

title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
statement: Design a class KthLargest that maintains the kth largest element in a data stream. The constructor takes (k, nums) with an initial array; add(val) appends val to the stream and returns the current kth largest element. Both initialization and each add call must be efficient for a long stream.
hints: You never need the whole stream — only the k largest elements seen so far.
A min-heap of size k keeps the kth largest at its top.
On add: push val, and if the heap exceeds k, pop the smallest.
approach: Maintain a min-heap containing exactly the k largest elements seen. Initialize by pushing all of nums and trimming to size k. On add(val), push val and pop if size exceeds k; the heap top is then the kth largest. Each add costs O(log k); init costs O(n log k).
complexity: Time O(log k) per add, O(n log k) init; space O(k).
pitfalls: Using a max-heap, which cannot evict the smallest of the top-k efficiently.
Forgetting to trim the heap during initialization when len(nums) > k.
Returning the heap top before trimming back to size k.

title: Last Stone Weight
statement: You are given an array of stone weights. Repeatedly take the two heaviest stones: if they are equal, both are destroyed; otherwise the heavier is reduced by the lighter's weight and put back. Continue until at most one stone remains, and return its weight (or 0 if none remain). Simulate this efficiently.
hints: You always need the two current maximums — that is exactly what a max-heap provides.
Pop twice, compute the difference, push it back only if nonzero.
Python's heapq is a min-heap: negate values to simulate a max-heap.
approach: Push all negated weights into a heap. While more than one stone remains: pop the two largest (most negative), and if they differ, push back their difference (negated). When the loop ends, return the negated top or 0. Each of the O(n) rounds costs O(log n).
complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n).
pitfalls: Pushing back a zero difference, causing an infinite loop.
Forgetting to negate when using a min-heap as a max-heap.
Re-sorting the array each round for O(n^2 log n) instead of using a heap.

title: The K Weakest Rows in a Matrix
statement: You are given an m x n binary matrix where each row is sorted (all 1s come before all 0s). A row's strength is its count of 1s; a row is weaker than another if it has fewer 1s, breaking ties by smaller row index. Return the indices of the k weakest rows, ordered from weakest to strongest.
hints: Because each row is sorted, a row's soldier count can be found with binary search — or just sum the row.
You need the k smallest (strength, index) pairs: a max-heap of size k works.
Simpler still: sort all rows by (count, index) and take the first k — O(m log m) is fine here.
approach: Compute each row's soldier count (sum, or binary search exploiting the sorted order). Collect (count, index) pairs, sort by count then index, and return the first k indices. Sorting dominates at O(m log m) with O(m*n) counting — easily fast enough, and a size-k heap gives O(m log k) alternatively.
complexity: Time O(m*n + m log m), space O(m).
pitfalls: Breaking ties incorrectly — weaker means smaller index on equal counts.
Counting 1s with a linear scan per row when binary search is available (minor).
Returning strengths instead of row indices.

title: Merge Sorted Array
statement: You are given two sorted integer arrays nums1 (with m elements followed by n zero slots) and nums2 (with n elements). Merge nums2 into nums1 in place so that nums1 becomes a single sorted array of length m + n. You must do this with O(1) extra space — merging from the front would overwrite unprocessed elements.
hints: Merging from the back avoids overwriting: the largest remaining element goes to the last free slot.
Use three pointers: i at the end of nums1's real data, j at the end of nums2, k at the very end.
After the main loop, any leftover nums2 elements still need copying; leftover nums1 elements are already in place.
approach: Three pointers from the back: i = m-1, j = n-1, k = m+n-1. While j >= 0, place max(nums1[i], nums2[j]) at k and decrement the used pointers. Elements remaining in nums1 are already correctly positioned. Single pass: O(m+n) time, O(1) space.
pitfalls: Merging front-to-back and clobbering nums1's unprocessed tail.
Forgetting to copy remaining nums2 elements when nums1 is exhausted first.
Off-by-one errors in the initial pointer positions.

title: Squares of a Sorted Array
statement: Given an integer array sorted in non-decreasing order, return an array of the squares of each number, also sorted in non-decreasing order. Squaring breaks the order because large negatives become large positives — but you can still do this in O(n) without a general sort.
hints: The largest square must come from one of the two ends (most negative or most positive).
Use two pointers at the ends, repeatedly taking the larger square and filling the result from the back.
This is the same two-pointer pattern as merging two sorted lists.
approach: Two pointers l = 0 and r = n-1, filling result from index n-1 downward: compare nums[l]^2 vs nums[r]^2, write the larger, and move that pointer inward. Each element is visited once: O(n) time, O(n) output space.
complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the output.
pitfalls: Squaring then calling sort — O(n log n) misses the intended linear solution.
Filling the result front-to-back, which reverses the order.
Integer overflow in languages with fixed-width ints (not an issue in Python).

title: Sort Array by Parity
statement: Given an integer array, rearrange it so that all even numbers come before all odd numbers, and return the array. The relative order within evens/odds does not matter. Do it in place with O(1) extra space if you can.
hints: This is a two-way partition, like one step of quicksort with pivot = oddness.
Two pointers from opposite ends: swap when the left points at an odd and the right at an even.
Alternatively, build the answer with a stable partition in O(n) extra space first.
approach: Two pointers l = 0, r = n-1: advance l past evens and r past odds; when l < r with nums[l] odd and nums[r] even, swap them. Each index is visited once: O(n) time, O(1) space.
pitfalls: Infinite loop when pointers are not advanced after a swap.
Using extra arrays when the in-place partition is straightforward.
Confusing this with a stable partition (order preservation is not required).

title: Number of Recent Calls
statement: Implement a RecentCounter class: ping(t) records a call at time t (milliseconds, strictly increasing) and returns the number of calls in the inclusive window [t - 3000, t]. Design ping to be efficient even after many calls — you should not rescan the entire history each time.
hints: Times are strictly increasing, so old calls leave the window forever in order.
A queue holds the call times; on each ping, drop from the front while older than t - 3000.
The queue's size after trimming is the answer.
approach: Keep a deque of timestamps. On ping(t): append t, then popleft while the front is < t - 3000. Return len(queue). Each timestamp is pushed and popped once across all calls: amortized O(1) per ping, O(n) space.
complexity: Amortized O(1) per ping, space O(n) for the window.
pitfalls: Rescanning all stored times per ping for O(n^2) total.
Using < vs <= on the window boundary [t-3000, t] (inclusive on both ends).
Using a list with pop(0), which is O(n) per pop — use collections.deque.

title: Implement Stack using Queues
statement: Implement a LIFO stack using only standard FIFO queue operations (push to back, peek/pop from front, size, isEmpty). Support push, pop, top, and empty. You may use two queues; make pop/top efficient and explain the trade-off versus the alternative layout.
hints: The trick is to keep the most recently pushed element at the FRONT of the main queue.
On push(x): enqueue x, then rotate the previous elements behind it.
After rotation, pop and top are plain queue operations.
approach: Single-queue version: push(x) enqueues x then dequeues-and-enqueues size-1 times, rotating older elements behind x so x is at the front. Then pop() and top() are O(1) queue ops, and push is O(n). The two-queue variant instead does the rotation lazily on pop.
complexity: Push O(n), pop/top/empty O(1); space O(n).
pitfalls: Rotating size times instead of size-1, putting x at the back again.
Forgetting that queue pop removes from the front, not the back.
Not handling pop/top on an empty stack.

title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
statement: You are given an integer array cost where cost[i] is the price of stepping on stair i. Starting from stair 0 or stair 1 for free, each move you may climb 1 or 2 stairs, paying the cost of the stair you land on. Find the minimum cost to reach the top (one step beyond the last stair).
hints: This is the same recurrence family as climbing-stairs, but with costs on landings.
dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]): the cheapest way to stand on stair i.
The answer is min(dp[n-1], dp[n-2]) since you can step off the top from either of the last two stairs.
approach: Define dp[i] as the minimum cost to reach stair i: dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]), with dp[0] = cost[0], dp[1] = cost[1]. The answer is min(dp[n-1], dp[n-2]). Keep two rolling variables for O(1) space.
pitfalls: Paying cost[0]/cost[1] for the starting stair (starting is free).
Returning dp[n-1] instead of min(dp[n-1], dp[n-2]).
Allocating a full dp array when two variables suffice.
